analysis.one_liner: Lets health care workers report patient safety problems without being fired, gagged, or bound by non-competes.
analysis.headline: A bill to protect health care workers who report unsafe staffing or care was introduced with no cosponsors and has not moved in any of its three committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar health care facilities from punishing workers who raise concerns about patient safety, staffing levels, or equipment. Workers would gain the right to sue for damages, including up to $1 million in punitive damages and class actions, gag clauses in contracts would become unenforceable, and whistleblowers would be released from non-compete agreements. Hospitals, nursing homes, and other Medicare providers would also have to set up anonymous reporting systems and investigate complaints to keep participating in Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care practitioners — nurses, doctors, aides, therapists, and others in any care setting from hospitals to dental offices — would gain a federal right to raise patient safety concerns without being fired, demoted, or pushed out, including concerns communicated to supervisors, state regulators, government officials, or patient safety organizations. Any adverse action within 180 days of a report would be presumed retaliation unless the employer proves otherwise. Retaliated workers could sue for actual damages, attorney's fees, and up to $1 million in punitive damages, and could join class actions covering facilities under common ownership. Gag clauses would be void, non-competes lifted, and safety reports shielded from use against workers in malpractice cases. Patients would benefit indirectly, as concerns about understaffing and unsafe conditions would have protected channels and Medicare providers would have to run anonymous reporting systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care workers who report unsafe care

how_it_helps.text: Bars health care facilities from retaliating against any practitioner who raises concerns about patient safety, staffing, or equipment — including to supervisors, state regulators, government officials, and patient safety organizations — and voids any contract clause that would gag such speech.

Gives retaliated workers a private right to sue for actual damages, attorney's fees, and up to $1 million in punitive damages, with class actions available across facilities under the same ownership or management.
Presumes that any adverse employment action within 180 days of a safety report is retaliation, shifting the burden of proof to the employer.
Releases whistleblowers from non-compete agreements tied to the facility and blocks their safety reports from being used to draw adverse conclusions about the care they provided in malpractice suits.
Requires Medicare providers to establish a mechanism for anonymous patient safety reports and a process for investigating them, as a condition of Medicare participation.

analysis.who_pays: Health care facilities — hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, and other providers — would bear damages awards, attorney's fees, and the cost of defending individual suits and class actions; staffing and management companies could also be pursued for contribution. Facilities would pay to build anonymous reporting and investigation systems. Those costs would fall on facility owners and operators, and to the extent they are passed through, on insurers and payers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and staffing companies

drawbacks.text: The enforcement design leans heavily toward litigation: punitive damages up to $1 million per case and class-action damages set at the greatest of actual damages, $500,000, or 1 percent of the facility owner's net worth would expose facilities — including financially struggling rural and safety-net hospitals — to large verdicts, and the bill holds a facility liable for retaliation by staffing or management companies it does not directly control.

The bill presumes that any adverse employment action within 180 days of a safety report is retaliation; even as a rebuttable presumption, this could deter legitimate performance management and push facilities toward defensive settlements.

Workers must first complain to state licensing authorities and, for hospitals, the Joint Commission, and must wait 90 days and see an earlier report fail before going to the news media — steps that could delay public warnings about urgent safety problems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real gap: health care workers today can face gag clauses, non-competes, and firing for speaking up about unsafe staffing or conditions, and the bill's presumption, damages, and class-action tools would give them genuine leverage. But the costs are real too — large statutory and punitive damages, a 180-day retaliation presumption, and liability attributed from contractors to facilities would raise legal costs across the sector, including at hospitals operating on thin margins. A narrower damages scheme would have traded some deterrence for less litigation burden; as written, the bill bets that aggressive lawsuits are the way to change facility behavior.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced; none has acted on it, and it sits with no cosponsors while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, and the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees for the portions each oversees.
Since that referral, no committee has taken the bill up, no vote has occurred, and no other member has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won anything yet. Health care facility operators continue under current law with no new liability, and if the bill dies in committee they will have avoided the litigation exposure and reporting requirements it would have imposed.

for.name: Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to three committees; no other member has joined as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split is on record; the only recorded obstacle is inaction — three committees have not scheduled any work on it.

industries.note: The bill creates a private right of action with punitive damages up to $1 million and class damages that can reach 1 percent of an owner's net worth, and makes facilities liable for retaliation by their own staff and contractors. Facilities would also have to operate anonymous reporting systems to keep Medicare participation.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care chains
industries.note: Nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities fall squarely within the bill's definition of a health care facility, and the class-action formula specifically reaches up to the net worth of parent entities that own multiple facilities — the structure of chain ownership in this sector.

Retaliation by a staffing company or management services firm would be attributed to the facility where it occurred, though those companies could be pursued for contribution afterward; their interest in avoiding liability runs against the public's interest in safe staffing.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since its April referral, the bill follows the most common path in Congress: death in committee. It would need cosponsors and a hearing or markup in at least one of its three committees before any floor vote, which is unlikely on this timeline; more probable is that it sits untouched until the Congress ends in January 2027.
